# Enantiomerically-Enriched a-Borylzinc Reagents by Nickel-Catalyzed Carbozincation of Vinylboronic Esters

**Authors:** Chenlong Zhang; Weipeng Hu; Gabriel J. Lovinger; Jing Jin; Jingjia Chen; James P. Morken

**Affiliations:** Department of Chemistry, Merkert Chemistry Center, Boston College, Chestnut Hill, Massachusetts 02467, United States

## Abstract

In this paper is described a synthesis of enantiomerically-enriched, configurationally stable organozinc reagents by catalytic enantioselective carbozincation of a vinylboronic ester. This process furnishes enantiomerically enriched α-borylzinc intermediates which are shown to undergo stereospecific reactions producing enantioenriched secondary boronic ester products. The properties of the intermediate α-borylzinc reagent are probed and the synthetic utility of the products is demonstrated by application to the synthesis of (−)-aphanorphine and (−)-enterolactone.

## Abstract

## INTRODUCTION

Since their first preparation in 1849,1 organozinc species have become versatile organometallic reagents.2 Because of their broad functional group compatibility, good configurational stability,3 and low toxicity, these reagents have been employed in a number of carbon–carbon and carbon–heteroatom bond forming reactions. While recent powerful reactions can employ racemic reagents for asymmetric synthesis,4,5 transition metal catalysis has further broadened the utility of non-racemic organozinc reagents. The most general method for the synthesis of organozinc reagents is zinc insertion into organic halides, however, the mechanism of this process involves free radical intermediates6 which renders asymmetric synthesis challenging. Alternative routes for the preparation of chiral organozinc reagents with high enantiomeric purity have been reported. Knochel developed an enantio- and diastereoselective hydroboration/boron–zinc exchange sequence (Figure 1a) and demonstrated that the resulting chiral organozinc reagents participate in a series of copper- or palladium-mediated stereospecific coupling reactions.7 More recently, Campos8 developed an enantioselective deprotonation/transmetallation method to prepare heterocycle-derived organozinc compounds (Fig. 1b), and this strategy was later modified by Gawley to employ catalytic amounts of lithiated diaminoalkoxide (Fig. 1c).9 Most recently, Knochel prepared chiral secondary organozinc reagents by stereoretentive lithium-halogen exchange followed by transmetallation (Fig. 1d),10 and showed that the resulting dialkylzinc reagent undergoes stereoretentive cross-coupling with C(sp2) electrophiles. In terms of catalytic synthesis, carbozincation of π bonds, which represents a unique branch of carbometallation11 reactions, provides an efficient route to organozinc reagents by the construction of carbon–carbon and carbon–zinc bonds in a single operation. Despite this intriguing reactivity, carbozincation of alkenes has rarely been reported. Although zirconium(II),12 iron(III)13 and tantalum(IV)14 complexes catalyze intermolecular carbozincation of terminal alkenes, enantioselective additions to alkenes have only been achieved with strained and reactive double bonds as seen in cyclopropenes (Fig. 1e)15 and [3.2.1] oxabicyclic alkenes.11d In this report, we describe a chiral Ni-based complex that facilitates enantioselective carbozincation of organoboronic esters, and show that under appropriate reaction conditions, the α-borylzinc products are configurationally stable and may couple with a wide range of electrophiles to furnish chiral alkyl boronic esters (Fig. 1f).16 The versatility of the resulting chiral boronic esters in stereospecific transformations17 offers a useful method for chemical synthesis.

## RESULTS AND DISCUSSION

Our efforts in development of an alkenylboronate carbozincation were inspired during studies on a Ni-catalyzed tandem radical addition/cross-coupling18 where products consistent with carbozincation were observed with some systems. Initial optimization of this process revealed nickel-L1 complex as prospective catalyst for the reaction of alkenylboronic ester 2 with phenylzinc chloride (3) in THF/DMSO/DMF solvent mixture at −40 °C (Table 1, entry 1). Notably, the reaction yields are generally improved by the inclusion of an alkyl iodide (0.5 to 2 equivalents, see Supporting Information for detailed optimization studies) which was anticipated to facilitate oxidation of low-valent inactive Ni species. After carbozincation, the α-borylzinc intermediate was subjected to copper(I)-mediated allylation followed by oxidation of the boronic ester, resulting in formation of homoallylic alcohol 4. The high enantiomeric purity of 4 suggests that the intermediate α-borylzinc reagent is not only configurationally stable during the reaction, but also reacts in a stereospecific fashion. Control experiments indicate that the nickel catalyst is indispensable for the reaction (entry 2 and 3) and the use of methyl iodide (vide infra) and a THF/DMF/DMSO solvent blend are important for the highest yield and enantioselectivity (entry 4–6). Use of the pinacol-derived boronic ester vinylB(pin) in place of vinylB(mac) resulted in diminished yield (entry 7, other alkenes such as styrene are unreactive). Of note, conducting the reaction at temperatures higher than −40 °C resulted in lower enantioselectivity (entry 8). Increasing the steric encumbrance of the ligand by installing substitution at the ortho position of the aryl ring increased the enantioselectivity but had a detrimental effect on reactivity (entry 9, 10).

With an effective reaction in hand, a selection of aryl zinc reagents was surveyed in the two-step carbozincation/allylation sequence with allyl bromide serving as the electrophile. Aryl nucleophiles bearing alkyl and aryl groups at meta and para positions are competent reaction partners (Fig. 2a, 5, 6, and 8). Functional groups such as a ketal, alkene, and alkyne, as well as a TBS-protected alcohol are tolerated (7 and 9–11). While aliphatic and alkenyl zinc reagents react with significantly diminished reactivity and/or selectivity, heterocycle- (12) and heteroatom-substituted (13-17) arylzinc reagents can also engage in the carbozincation process providing the chiral alcohols with moderate to good yield and enantiomeric purity. A number of different electrophiles were also examined as trapping reagents for the carbozincation adduct. Allyl chlorides and bromides with a variety of functional groups and substitution patterns were subjected to the reaction and found to be effective (Fig. 2b). Unprotected alcohols (29) and amines (24) can be tolerated and did not lead to competitive protonation of the C–Zn species. It was also shown that a conjugated enone (26) and enyne (27) can be generated with high diastereoselectivity. Synthetically useful structures such as an alkenyl halide (28), alkenyl boronic ester (30), and an allyl acetate (31) can also be synthesized from readily available materials. In addition to allyl electrophiles, propargyl chloride is suitable for this reaction and furnishes homoallenyl alcohol 32 with equally good yield and selectivity. Also of note, the α-borylzinc reagents can engage in stereospecific palladium-catalyzed Negishi cross-coupling with alkenyl (33) or aryl (34) iodides, preserving the enantiomeric enrichment of the boron-substituted stereogenic center. In this process, the use of lithium chloride as an additive was found to be crucial for preserving enantiomeric enrichment during the cross-coupling. Lastly, enantiospecific bromination and chlorination (Br2 and trichloroisocyanuric acid/CeCl3 respectively), furnished enantiomerically enriched α-haloboronates (35 and 36). That α-halo boronates participate in stereoinvertive substitution reactions with carbon- and nitrogen-based nucleophiles provides a useful strategy for further elaboration of these motifs.19 Interestingly, the absolute configurations of the halogenation products (35 and 36) are opposite to the compounds obtained from the allylation and cross-coupling reactions.

The synthetic utility of the carbozincation products was probed by examining additional transformations and applications in natural product synthesis. In one experiment, it was shown that γ-butyrolactone 37, a compound used by Hoveyda and coworkers20 as an intermediate towards the synthesis of bruguierol A, could be accessed from bis(boronate) 30 by successive oxidation with sodium perborate and then PCC (Fig. 3a). Also of note, while direct conjugate addition of the α-borylzinc reagent has not yet been accomplished, allylation product 28 can be oxidized to an equivalent product, γ-siloxy ester 38 by cobalt-mediated oxidation (Fig. 3b).21 That the carbozincation/trap sequence can accommodate unprotected meth-oxyamines, allows production of 24, which was found to be a substrate for intramolecular stereospecific amination22 reaction to give pyrrolidine derivative 39 (Fig. 3c). In a short sequence, 39 could be converted to (−)-aphanorphine23 (40) by Friedel-Crafts cyclization, palladium-catalyzed hydroxylation,24 and LAH reduction. This new strategy currently provides the shortest published route to this target. Lastly, it was found that boronic ester 17-B could be converted to chiral alcohol 42 through a Matteson homologation (Fig. 3d), and this compound (42) serves as a convenient precursor to the lignan natural product (−)-enterolactone25 (45) by oxidative lactonization, diastereoselective alkylation, and demethylation26.

The intriguing reactivity described above prompted us to probe the reaction mechanism and several observations pointed to the inner-workings of the catalytic cycle. First, electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) data was collected for a reaction under standard conditions (Fig. 4a). Simulation of the spectrum suggests that it contains a mixture of an (L1)Ni(I)–Cl complex (g⊥=2.324, g∥=2.002) and a (L1)Ni(I)–C complex (g⊥=2.370, g∥=2.004) with the best fit to experimental data being with a 68:32 ratio of these species. Comparison of the abundance of Ni(I) species with the reaction progress at multiple time points (Fig. 4b) showed the ratio of Ni(I) relative to other species is high during the period with highest reaction rate (i.e., in the first 8 hours), whereas a low percentage of Ni(I) species was observed when the reaction progressed at a lower rate. While this comparison doesn’t necessarily rule out the activity of a small concentration of other highly reactive Ni species, it does suggest Ni(I) complexes as plausible catalysts. A second mechanistic clue was found in the formation of enantiomerically-enriched methyl-containing compound 46 which was obtained as a byproduct of the reaction (Fig. 4c, eq. 1). To learn about the origin of 46, the carbozincation reaction was directly subjected to protic work-up whereupon compound 46 was still obtained in addition to primary alcohol 47 (eq. 2); this observation indicates that the byproduct does not arise from copper(I)-mediated methylation. Of note, maintaining the carbozincation reaction for an extended time at elevated temperature and in the presence of excess methyl iodide did not increase the yield of 46 (eq. 3), suggesting that 46 does not form by direct electrophilic trap of the α-borylzinc reagent with methyl iodide. When primary alkyl iodides with increased steric hindrance were employed in place of methyl iodide, diminished reactivity was observed, yet the selectivity of the carbozincation reaction remained constant (Fig. 4d). This result suggests the alkyl group of the iodoalkane does not serve as a spectator ligand on the Ni complex during the stereochemistry-determining step of the process. Lastly, when trans-deuterio vinyl boronic ester 50 was subjected to the standard conditions, net syn addition to the alkene was observed in both the carbozincation/allylation product (51), in the methylation byproduct (52) (Fig. 4e, eq. 1), as well as in the carbozincation/Negishi coupling product (53). The stereochemical outcome of these processes suggests the carbozincation occurs by concerted β-migratory insertion rather than aryl radical addition to vinylB(mac).

Collectively, the observations above may be accounted for by a catalytic cycle where carbozincation with an aryl–Ni(I) complex (I → II → III, Fig. 4f) occurs, and that methylation byproduct 46 is generated by oxidative addition/reductive elimination involving an organonickel(III) intermediate such as IV (Fig. 4f). Following this scenario, the absolute configuration of the methyl-containing byproduct (46) likely reflects the configuration of the organonickel intermediate. Under this mechanism the carbozincation occurs in a redox neutral fashion by olefin insertion and subsequent transmetallation with an arylzinc halide. The requisite generation of Ni(I) complexes from the NiBr2 precatalyst can occur by a number of different mechanisms, but to our knowledge the generation of (diamine)Ni(I) complexes has not been closely studied. Experimental work on related diphosphine27, bipyridine28, and pincer-based systems29 suggests that mechanisms involving conversion of a fraction of Ni(II) to Ni(0), followed by comproportionation, can provide Ni(I) species. Alternatively, bimetallic oxidative addition may convert Ni(II) complexes to Ni(III) species and these, in turn, may be converted to Ni(I) by reductive elimination30 (see dashed box, Fig. 4f). To probe this possibility, 3-methoxyphenylzinc chloride and 3-phenylpropyl iodide were employed in a coupling reaction (Fig. 4g). In addition to carbozincation products, cross-coupling product 48 and homocoupling product 49 were isolated in 10% and 7% yield, respectively. The formation of both of these compounds is consistent with bimetallic oxidative addition as a route to Ni(I) and given the marked positive impact of alkyl iodides on the carbozincation reaction, we expect that the bimetallic oxidative addition is the more likely path to catalyst activation.

The ability of the enantioselective carbozincation to provide a useful route to non-racemic chiral building blocks, outside of the transformations presented in the examples above, will rely on an understanding of the configurational stability of the α-borylzinc intermediate. To learn more about this feature of the α-borylzinc compounds, carbozincation of deuterium-labeled vinylB(mac) 50 was conducted and the configurational stability of the labeled α-borylzinc compound 54 was monitored by 1H NMR at different temperatures. As shown in Fig. 4h, the diastereomeric excess of 54 remained constant when the compound was maintained at −10 °C for 3 hours. Epimerization is more rapid at 5 °C, and at 40 °C complete scrambling occurs within 10 minutes. Thus, effective use of these reagents in asymmetric synthesis appears to require rigorous maintenance of low temperature reaction conditions, however, we note that the addition of LiCl allows stereospecificity in Negishi couplings at higher temperatures and expect that this additive may be of use in other contexts.

## CONCLUSION

In summary, a catalytic enantioselective carbozincation of vinylboronic esters furnishes enantioenriched α-borylzinc reagents. The chiral α-borylzinc reagents can be directly converted to chiral boronic esters by copper(I)-mediated or palladium(II)-catalyzed coupling reactions or by halogenation reactions in a stereospecific fashion. Mechanistic studies with deterium-labeled substrate and EPR experiments revealed a plausible catalytic cycle involving a nickel(I) complex that catalyzes the carbozincation reaction in a redox neutral fashion. Efforts to extend this process to other alkenes and other organozinc reagents are ongoing.
